A0232.title: Robot Safety Stop E-stop & Functional-Safety Design
keywords: robot safety stop E-stop & functional-safety design
A0232.definition: Hardware-level emergency-stop loops, safety controllers, collaborative-robot force and speed limits, and ISO 10218/ISO/TS 15066 compliant functional-safety design to ensure robots can stop quickly and limit physical harm under anomalies.
A0232.description: Robot safety E-stop and functional safety design addresses risks of physical harm and functional safety failures by establishing a defense-in-depth approach spanning hardware to architecture. First, a hardware-level emergency stop circuit operates independently of software control paths, cutting off motive power immediately when pressed, so software faults cannot bypass it. Second, safety controllers employ redundant architectures and self-diagnostics to perform safety interlock monitoring (light curtains, safety mats, safety gates). Third, collaborative robot force and speed limits comply with ISO/TS 15066 human-robot collaboration force/pressure thresholds, actively decelerating before a collision. Fourth, functional safety design follows ISO 10218 for industrial robot safety and ISO 13482 for personal care robot safety, conducting risk assessments and designing to safety integrity levels (PLd/SIL2). This measure serves as the core physical safety line after incidents such as the Knightscope K5 collision and the Volkswagen Baunatal robot fatality, and works in conjunction with A0147 (industrial protocol security hardening) and A0014 (tamper-proof mechanisms); the former focuses on communication protocol security, while this measure focuses on physical-layer functional safety.
A0232.limitation: Hardware emergency stops cannot counteract mechanical inertia once force is already applied, and high-speed motion still requires a braking distance before stopping. Functional safety certification involves high cost and long lead times, making it difficult for small and medium-sized enterprises to afford. Software-based emergency stops can be bypassed by software faults, so hardware emergency stops must serve as the ultimate fallback. Force and speed limits reduce task efficiency, requiring fine-tuning in collaborative scenarios.
